```{r}
#| label: setup

suppressMessages(library(gt))

# Shared dark-canvas table theme, matching the deck (teal header, light text).
# Tables sit on the dark canvas, so the table background is transparent and
# text is the ink-light #F1EEE6; accent borders use the indigo #4A5899.
gt_dark <- function(tbl, font_size = 20) {
  gt(tbl) |>
    tab_options(
      table.background.color = "transparent",
      table.font.color = "#F1EEE6",
      table.font.size = px(font_size),
      data_row.padding = px(7),
      column_labels.background.color = "#2E7D6B",
      column_labels.padding = px(9),
      table.border.top.color = "transparent",
      table.border.top.style = "none",
      table.border.bottom.color = "transparent",
      table.border.bottom.style = "none",
      table_body.border.top.color = "#4A5899",
      table_body.border.bottom.color = "transparent",
      table_body.border.bottom.style = "none",
      column_labels.border.top.color = "transparent",
      column_labels.border.top.style = "none",
      column_labels.border.bottom.color = "#17251F",
      heading.background.color = "transparent",
      heading.border.bottom.color = "#17251F"
    ) |>
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(color = "#F1EEE6", weight = "600"),
      locations = cells_column_labels()
    ) |>
    tab_style(
      style = cell_borders(
        sides = "bottom",
        color = "rgba(241,238,230,0.22)",
        weight = px(1)
      ),
      locations = cells_body()
    ) |>
    fmt_markdown(everything())
}
```

# Welcome

## Welcome {.center}

::: {.big-title style="left:96px; top:200px; width:1100px; font-size:64px;"}
Interactive reports without a server
:::

::: {style="position:absolute; left:96px; top:420px; width:1100px; font-size:26px; color:rgba(241,238,230,0.85);"}
A hands-on introduction to **Quarto** and **Shinylive**, from reproducible documents to fully interactive reports served from a plain static web page.
:::

## Who is this for?

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**You already know.**]{.hl-draft} R is your daily tool, and R Markdown is second nature.

[**You will consolidate.**]{.hl-review} Quarto: the modern, RMarkdown-compatible successor, with a lighter learning curve than you might fear.

[**You will discover.**]{.hl-release} Shiny's reactive model, then Shinylive: the same Shiny apps running entirely in the browser, with no R server at all.
:::

## Today's goals

By the end of this workshop you will walk away able to:

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**Quarto.**]{.hl-draft} Map everything you know from R Markdown onto Quarto, the modern successor.

[**Shiny.**]{.hl-review} Build a small interactive app and grasp its reactive core.

[**Shinylive.**]{.hl-release} Export that app to a standalone static page, and embed Shiny in a Quarto report hosted on GitHub Pages, with no server.

[**Choose.**]{.hl-wrap} Weigh the trade-offs and pick the right engine for each job.
:::

## Housekeeping

Everything today runs **locally**: a browser and your IDE, with no server to set up or maintain.

::: {.house-grid}
<div class="house">[**Nothing new to install.**]{.hl-draft} R plus Quarto's render, in RStudio or Positron, exactly as you already work.</div>

<div class="house">[**No remote service until the end.**]{.hl-release} We only deploy a static page in the very last step.</div>

<div class="house">[**Falling behind?**]{.hl-review} The finished examples live in `apps/penguins-app/`. Copy the answer and keep going.</div>

<div class="house">[**Ask any time.**]{.hl-wrap} The Shiny section is paced deliberately slower, so questions are welcome throughout.</div>
:::

## A gentle introduction to Positron

**Positron** is an open source data science IDE from Posit. If you use RStudio, everything today works identically.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Why try it

- A **fork of VS Code**: first-class editor, fast console, R and Python side by side.
- **Quarto** built in: render from the toolbar, one-click slide preview.
- Same shortcuts as RStudio (`Ctrl/Cmd+Enter`).

### How to get it

- Download from <https://positron.posit.co>, open it like RStudio.
- Pick your R interpreter on first launch (it auto-detects).
- The labs are IDE-neutral: stay in RStudio or drop in.

:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Not a sales pitch.** A modern, free editor with strong Quarto support.
:::

## From R Markdown to Quarto

Quarto is a **multi-language scientific and technical publishing system** built by Posit.
If you know R Markdown, you already know 80% of Quarto.

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**Same ideas.**]{.hl-draft} Markdown + code chunks + YAML front matter, rendered to many output formats.

[**Same engine.**]{.hl-review} R code still runs through knitr; only the chunk-option syntax changes (`{r, echo=}` → `#| echo:` lines).

[**Same workflow.**]{.hl-release} Write a `.qmd`, click Render / `quarto render`, get HTML, PDF or slides.
:::

## Similarities with R Markdown

Most of what you already know carries straight over. With a few renames:

::: {.incremental .highlight-last}
- **Chunk syntax.** Same three backticks and `{r}`: `` ```{r} `` starts a chunk, unchanged.
- **Chunk options.** Now written one per line, `#| key: value`. Or keep the old `{r, echo=TRUE}` header form.
- **YAML front matter.** Same fields; only `output:` becomes `format:`.
- **Inline R in prose.** <code>&#96;r 2 + 2&#96;</code> still evaluates at render.
- **One source, many formats.** HTML, PDF, docx, revealjs and more.
:::

::: {.small-note}
References: [execution options](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html) · [front matter](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/front-matter.html) · [output formats](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html)
:::

## A minimal Quarto example

A minimal Quarto document is barely more than YAML + one code chunk.

::: {style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; gap:24px; margin-top:12px;"}
::: {.codewindow .md width="100%"}
hello.qmd
```{.markdown include="../examples/hello.qmd"}
```
:::

::: {style="border:1px solid rgba(241,238,230,0.25); border-radius:8px; overflow:hidden; height:430px; background:#fff;"}
<iframe src="examples/hello.html" style="width:100%; height:100%; border:0;" title="Rendered hello.qmd"></iframe>
:::
:::

**Render** is one click. `#| label:` names the figure for a cross-reference.

## Differences that matter

The same skeleton, but the moving parts have names and defaults:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diff
#| tbl-cap: "R Markdown vs Quarto at a glance"
#| echo: false
gt_dark(data.frame(
  Aspect     = c("Languages", "Output", "Chunk options", "Projects", "Slides"),
  `R Markdown (.Rmd)` = c("R, via knitr",
                          "`output:` in YAML",
                          "`{r, echo=FALSE}` header",
                          "`_site.yml` for websites",
                          "`xaringan`, `slidy`, `ioslides`"),
  `Quarto (.qmd)`     = c("Same R, plus Python, Julia, OJS",
                          "`format:` in YAML",
                          "`#| echo: false` lines (old form still works)",
                          "`_quarto.yml`, first-class for any project",
                          "Native `format: revealjs`"),
  check.names = FALSE
), font_size = 24)
```

::: {.callout-note}
The useful habit: treat Quarto as **RMarkdown that grew up**. Nothing you know is wasted; most of it just got a new name.
:::

## Quarto projects

A folder with a `_quarto.yml` becomes a **project**: one file configuring the whole
folder. Four built-in **types** -- `website`, `book`, `manuscript`, or `default`.

::: {.codewindow .yaml width="100%"}
_quarto.yml
```yaml
project:
  type: default        # default | website | book | manuscript
output-dir: _output
execute:
  freeze: true         # cache results, rerun only when inputs change

format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: cosmo
```
:::

`quarto preview` rebuilds + live-reloads project as you edit; `quarto render` builds final output; `quarto publish` deploys it. See the [project reference](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/quarto-projects.html).

## One brand, everywhere

A `_brand.yml` at the project root carries **colors, fonts and logo** in one place; one change re-skins every report, deck and app.

::: {.codewindow .yaml width="90%"}
_brand.yml
```yaml
color:
  palette:
    teal: "#2E7D6B"
    amber: "#E8A33D"
  primary: teal
  secondary: amber
typography:
  base: Inter
  fonts:
    - family: Inter
```
:::

Apply it via the `brand` key, or let Quarto/Shiny auto-discover `_brand.yml`. See the
[brand reference](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/brand.html).

## Render targets

Quarto renders many formats from the same source. The key commands:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-targets
#| tbl-cap: "Same source, many targets"
#| echo: false
gt_dark(data.frame(
  Command = c("Render button",
              "`quarto render f.qmd --to html`",
              "`quarto preview`",
              "`quarto render --to revealjs`"),
  Output  = c("The format in YAML `format:`",
              "Force a specific format",
              "Live-reload preview",
              "A slide deck from a folder")
))
```

::: {.hands-on}
**Quick check.** Open `examples/` and render the `hello.qmd` example to HTML. Confirm the output file appears next to the source.
:::

## From R Markdown to Quarto in practice

Converting existing analysis is mechanical. Same code, few renamed keys:

::: {style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr; gap:24px; margin-top:14px;"}
::: {.codewindow .md width="100%"}
analysis.Rmd
```{.markdown include="examples/analysis.Rmd"}
```
:::

::: {.codewindow .md width="100%"}
analysis.qmd
```{.markdown include="examples/analysis.qmd"}
```
:::
:::

- `output:` becomes nested `format:`.
- `{r, opt=}` headers become `#| opt:` lines.
- Live Shiny: Rmd's `runtime: shiny` is renamed to `server: shiny` in Qmd.

Quarto can emphasise a note, a tip, a warning with a **callout** (fenced div with a `callout-*` class). Five built-ins: `note`, `tip`, `important`, `warning`, `caution`.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

## Why Quarto for our purpose

For this workshop, Quarto matters for **three** reasons that build toward the final goal:

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**Structured reports.**]{.hl-draft} Text, code and figures interleaved in one reproducible document.

[**Embedded interactivity.**]{.hl-review} Either live Shiny (`server: shiny` in Qmd) on a server, or Shinylive blocks (or Observable JS) that run in the browser.

[**Static output.**]{.hl-release} A rendered Quarto HTML page is plain files, ready for any static host.
:::

## Hands-on bandwidth {.light background-color="#F1EEE6"}

::: {.hands-on}
**Now open `labs/lab-01-quarto.qmd`** and work through it. It covers:

1. Writing your first `.qmd` and choosing an output format.
2. Structure, headings, lists, code chunks and inline code.
3. A comparison table of `.Rmd` vs `.qmd` chunk options.
4. Adding a caption and cross-referencing a figure.
:::

## Summary so far

- Quarto = **RMarkdown, generalised**: Python, Julia and Observable join R.
- Projects (`_quarto.yml`) centralise config; one source, many formats.
- Rendered output is plain files → a perfect fit for static hosting later.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why Quarto V2"}
- **Instant start.** A single self-contained binary; launches and renders faster.
- **Native PDF, no LaTeX.** Embedded Typst engine: polished PDFs from plain text.
- **Live authoring.** Hot reload and fast incremental renders while you edit.
- **Collaborative.** Live-preview session links for real-time team co-editing.
- **Backwards compatible.** Quarto 1 projects and extensions keep working.
:::

## What Shiny is

Shiny is a framework for **interactive web applications**: you write an app in R, and
Shiny serves it as a web page that reacts to the reader's actions. It is not a purely
R idea -- later we note the Python flavour -- but we go through R throughout today.

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**UI.**]{.hl-draft} The layout: sliders, buttons, tables, plots, text.

[**Server.**]{.hl-review} The logic: what happens when the user changes an input.

[**Reactive wiring.**]{.hl-release} What Shiny calls the "reactive graph": inputs flow to outputs.
:::

## A minimal Shiny app

Every Shiny app has two pieces. The smallest possible app:

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
app.R
```r
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sliderInput(inputId = "n", label = "Number of points",
              min = 10, max = 200, value = 50),
  textOutput(outputId = "msg")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$msg <- renderText({
    paste("You chose", input$n, "points")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```
:::

Run it with **Run App** (or `shiny::runApp("app.R")`).

## The reactive model, visually

Shiny tracks dependencies so only what changed re-renders.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  I["input$n (slider)"] --> R["reactive expression<br/>computed once, cached"]
  R --> M["output$msg<br/>renderText"]
  R --> P["output$plot<br/>renderPlot"]
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Reactive flow**:

- input change invalidates expressions that read it, which in turn invalidate outputs that depend on them
- Shiny recomputes only that minimal set.

**Reactive expression**: compute a value once + cache it $\rightarrow$ dependent outputs
reuse a single computation.
:::

## Inputs you will use today

Shiny ships a rich widget set. The four you will rely on for the labs:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-inputs
#| tbl-cap: "The four input widgets you will rely on"
#| echo: false
gt_dark(data.frame(
  Widget   = c("Slider", "Select", "Checkbox", "File upload"),
  Function = c("`sliderInput(\"id\", \"N\", 0, 100, 30)`",
               "`selectInput(\"id\", \"Var\", choices)`",
               "`checkboxInput(\"id\", \"Label\")`",
               "`fileInput(\"id\", \"CSV\")`"),
  Returns  = c("one number",
               "one (or more) values",
               "TRUE / FALSE",
               "a file handle, read with `read.csv(input$id$datapath)`")
), font_size = 24)
```

Need a different widget? See the [full list of UI inputs](https://shiny.posit.co/r/getstarted/build-an-app/reactive-flow/ui-inputs.html).

## Output functions and renderers

```{r}
#| label: tbl-output
#| tbl-cap: "Output functions and their paired renderers"
#| echo: false
gt_dark(data.frame(
  `Output function` = c("`textOutput()`", "`plotOutput()`", "`tableOutput()`", "`uiOutput()`"),
  `Paired renderer` = c("`renderText()`", "`renderPlot({})`", "`renderTable()` / `renderDT()`", "`renderUI()`"),
  Example           = c("`paste0(...)`", "a ggplot", "data frame", "dynamically built UI"),
  check.names = FALSE
), font_size = 24)
```

A rule of thumb: **every `render*()` function turns an R value into the HTML its paired
output function displays**.

More [UI outputs](https://shiny.posit.co/r/getstarted/build-an-app/reactive-flow/ui-outputs.html)
and [render functions](https://shiny.posit.co/r/getstarted/build-an-app/reactive-flow/render-functions.html).

## A reactive app with a plot

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
app.R
```r
library(shiny); library(ggplot2); library(dplyr)
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Palmer penguins explorer"),
  fileInput("data", "Upload your data (CSV)", accept = ".csv"),
  sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins", 5, 40, 20),
  plotOutput("hist")
)
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  peng <- reactive({ req(input$data); readr::read_csv(input$data$datapath) })
  output$hist <- renderPlot({
    peng() |> ggplot(aes(body_mass_g)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = input$bins, fill = "#2E7D6B")
  })
}
shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

`reactive({})` reads the file once, then re-runs only when the upload changes. Run it at `apps/penguins-app/app.R`.

## Reactive details that trip people up

**Reactives are lazy and cached**: a `reactive({})` recomputes only when its inputs change.

::: {.incremental .highlight-last}
- **`req()` guards**: `req(input$x)` halts until `input$x` is non-empty, avoiding errors on first render.
- **`eventReactive()`**: for click-driven actions (button → go), when you do not want recomputation on every keystroke.
- **Side-effects live in observers or `render*()`**: a `reactive()` only computes a value. To *do* something when an input changes -- a `showNotification()`, refreshed `updateSelectInput()` choices, a revealed panel -- use an observer (`observe()`) or an output.
:::

## Shiny inside a Quarto document

"Shiny in Quarto" covers **two very different setups**; keep them apart. The classic,
server-backed route first:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Live (server-backed)

`server: shiny` in the YAML serves a live app from an **R process**, so it needs a server (Old R Markdown `runtime: shiny` became `server: shiny` in Shiny).

```yaml
---
title: "My live app"
format: html
server: shiny
---
```

App code goes in **regular `{r}` chunks**; the reactive logic sits in an `{r}` chunk (plain for UI elements, with `#| context: server` option for server).

### Static (Shinylive, our goal)

The YAML loads the shinylive **filter**, so no server is involved.

```yaml
---
title: "My interactive report"
format: html
filters:
  - shinylive
---
```

App code goes in **`{shinylive-r}` chunks**. We write our first one in the next block.

:::

## Hands-on bandwidth {.light background-color="#F1EEE6"}

::: {.hands-on}
**Work through `labs/lab-02-shiny.qmd`.** It builds your first Shiny app step by step:

1. The two-piece skeleton (UI + server), run it with **Run App**.
2. Add an input and a text output and turn it into a histogram.
3. Add a second input (a `selectInput`) and a reactive expression.
4. (Stretch) Update UI elements dynamically.
5. (Stretch) Handle an uploaded CSV with `fileInput` and `readr::read_csv`.
:::

## Summary and breakthrough

- Shiny = **UI + server** wired through a **reactive graph**.
- Inputs change → reactives recompute → outputs re-render, minimally.
- `req()` and `reactive()` keep apps robust and lean.
- In Quarto, **`server: shiny`** needs a server; our goal is the **static** route.

::: {.callout-tip title="Shiny is not just R"}
A **Python** flavour of Shiny exists too, with the same ideas in another language.
:::

So the question: what if we **shipped the app itself** to the reader's browser instead of hosting
it on an R process? That is **Shinylive** (WebAssembly, webR, and a web asset library), which is next up.

## Why host without a server?

Shiny traditionally needs a **server program** running around the clock, which takes time, expertise and
money to keep up.

Shinylive is the alternative: the whole app becomes **plain files** that any
static host can serve, so the browser does the computing.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Non-static (server)

- A **server program** computes and streams results; any package, secret keys; costs money and maintenance.

### Static (Shinylive, GitHub Pages, Netlify)

- The host just serves **files**; the **reader's browser** runs the app. Free and fast; but WASM-only, no secret keys.

:::

## The three tools behind Shinylive

Three tools, one idea: run R in the browser with no server.

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**WebAssembly.**]{.hl-draft} A portable, **sandboxed binary** format. Sandboxed: it runs isolated from your computer and the page. Binary: it is compiled machine code in a `.wasm` file, not human-readable source. Browsers run it at near-native speed.

[**webR.**]{.hl-review} The R interpreter compiled to WebAssembly, so R runs inside the browser.

[**Web assets library.**]{.hl-release} A bundle of static JS/CSS/files a page downloads and runs; Shinylive itself is one.
:::

## What is WebAssembly?

**WebAssembly (WASM)** is a low-level **bytecode**: the machine-readable instructions a browser
executes, run inside a secure sandbox. Think of it as a "portable CPU" that every browser
already includes.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The idea

- Languages like C, C++, Rust, R are **compiled to `.wasm` files**.
- The browser runs them at near-native speed, isolated from the page.
- It powers heavy in-browser apps: softs and web apps (Google Earth, AutoCAD, TensorFlow), games (Unity 3D engine, Doom, GameBoy), smartphone apps, and now statistical computing.

### Why it matters here

- R is normally an installed binary. WASM lets the same R run **wherever a browser runs**:
  a phone, a colleague's computer, GitHub Pages.
- No server is needed to interpret the code; the browser is the runtime.

:::

::: {.small-note}
Sources: [webassembly.org](https://webassembly.org) · [developer's guide](https://webassembly.org/getting-started/developers-guide/)
:::

## What is webR?

**webR** is the R interpreter recompiled to WebAssembly, so R runs entirely in the browser. The recipe builds R for the browser in one line:

::: {style="margin:8px auto 0; padding:14px 22px; border:1px solid rgba(241,238,230,0.28); border-radius:12px; background:rgba(241,238,230,0.06); text-align:center;"}
$$\mathrm{webR} = \mathrm{R} + \mathrm{WASM} + \mathrm{Node.js} + \mathrm{Emscripten}$$
:::

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**WASM.**]{.hl-draft} The new "hardware": the portable binary every browser executes.

[**Node.js.**]{.hl-review} The build kitchen: the JS toolchain that assembles R for the web.

[**Emscripten.**]{.hl-release} The compiler bridge: pure R ports easily, but its C/C++ core needs turning into WASM, which is where Emscripten comes in.
:::

## webR in action

- Your **R packages** are compiled to WASM too, available from the webR repository: <https://repo.r-wasm.org>
- Popular packages (tidyverse, ggplot2, dplyr, readr) work.
- webR lets a page call R from JavaScript and render results live.
- Project home: <https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/>

::: {.callout-warning}
**A package must already be compiled to WASM** to run in the browser. Only packages listed in
the webR repository (<https://repo.r-wasm.org>) work out of the box.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Sweet spot.** webR means "the same R you use at your desk, inside the reader's tab". The data never
leaves their computer, and the code they see is the code you wrote.
:::

## What is a web assets library?

A **web assets library** is a set of static files (JavaScript, CSS, worker scripts, WASM
binaries) a page downloads and runs. **Shinylive** is exactly one: it bundles the machinery to
run Shiny in the browser via webR, as files you can drop on any static host.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Shinylive, the R package

`shinylive::export()` turns a local Shiny app into a self-contained static folder:

::: {.codewindow .r width="75%"}
export.R
```r
shinylive::export("app", "site")  # app folder -> static site/
```
:::

### The Quarto extension

`quarto add quarto-ext/shinylive` runs Shiny inside a report via a filter:

::: {.codewindow .yaml width="75%"}
_quarto.yml
```yaml
filters:
  - shinylive
```
:::

### Try it online

Copy-paste a ready-made app to see one running in your browser:

- Examples: <https://shinylive.io/r/examples/>

:::

::: {.small-note}
Sources: [R package site](https://posit-dev.github.io/r-shinylive/) · [online examples](https://shinylive.io/r/examples/) · [0.8.0 blog post](https://tidyverse.org/blog/2024/10/shinylive-0-8-0/)
:::

## What the browser downloads

On first open, the browser pulls down a bundle once:

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**webR / WASM binaries.**]{.hl-draft} The R interpreter run in the browser.

[**Shiny + Shinylive assets.**]{.hl-review} The framework and glue.

[**Your app's code & packages.**]{.hl-release} Your UI/server, plus WASM packages.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
This bundle is the main cost of Shinylive: a "cold start" may take a few seconds on first load; later visits are cached by the browser.
:::

---

## Route 1: a Shiny app, hosted static

Our first serverless goal: take a **standalone Shiny app** and host it on a static site.
The route, in one picture:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[app.R] --> B[shinylive::export]
  C[R packages → WASM] --> B
  D[Shinylive web assets] --> B
  B --> E[static site folder]
  E --> F[any static host]
```

## Export, in practice

Take the penguins app from the Shiny block. Exporting it is two lines:

::: {.codewindow .r width="70%"}
export.R
```r
shinylive::export("apps/penguins-app", "site")
httpuv::runStaticServer("site")
```
:::

- `shinylive::export(appdir, destdir)` walks your app folder;
- resolves the R packages it needs,
- downloads the Shinylive web assets; and,
- writes a self-contained static site into `destdir`.

The result is plain files: drop them on GitHub Pages, Netlify, or any static host.

## Pinning versions for the browser

`shinylive::export` figures out the **R packages** your app calls and bundles their WASM
builds. For deployments that keep working, pin the versions:

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
[**With renv.**]{.hl-draft} `renv::init()` once writes a `renv.lock`; `renv::snapshot()` captures updates
to it as you change packages. `shinylive::export` reads the lockfile and ships those exact WASM
builds, the most reproducible path: the browser gets the same versions you tested.

[**Without renv.**]{.hl-review} It scans your dependencies and uses the **latest** webR
builds. Fragile: a future package update can silently break a deployed app.
:::

## Try it now {.light background-color="#F1EEE6"}

::: {.hands-on}
**In `labs/lab-03-shinylive.qmd`:**

1. Run `shinylive::export("apps/penguins-app", "site")`.
2. Serve locally with `httpuv::runStaticServer("site")` and open the URL. Confirm app runs in your browser, with **no R server involved**.
3. Inspect exported `site/` folder: notice the payload files (WASM, JS).
4. Optional: upload your own CSV and confirm **no network request** carries it (check the Network tab: the file never leaves).
:::

---

## Route 2: Shiny inside a Quarto report

Our second serverless goal: turn a **Quarto report** into an **interactive page** where the
charts themselves are Shiny apps, all within one static document.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[report.qmd] --> B[quarto-ext/shinylive]
  C[shinylive-r blocks] --> B
  B --> E[static report.html]
  E --> F[any static host]
```

Install the extension, then enable its filter:

::: {.codewindow width="75%"}
::: {.editor .bash name="terminal"}
```bash
quarto add quarto-ext/shinylive
```
:::

::: {.editor .yaml .fragment name="_quarto.yml"}
```yaml
format: html

filters:
  - shinylive
```
:::
:::

## Anatomy of an interactive block

Wrap a complete Shiny app in a `{shinylive-r}` code block: the rest of the page is static, the block becomes a live self-contained app.

````yaml
---
title: "Interactive report"
format: html
filters:
  - shinylive
---
````

````markdown
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor]
library(shiny)
ui <- fluidPage(
  sliderInput("n", "Samples", 10, 500, 100),
  plotOutput("hist")
)
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$hist <- renderPlot(hist(rnorm(input$n), col = "#2E7D6B"))
}
shinyApp(ui, server)
```
````

## A full interactive report pattern

A realistic report mixes prose, static figures, tables, and one or more `{shinylive-r}` widgets:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Report structure

- Narrative sections with **static** text and figures.
- A `{shinylive-r}` block for each interactive tool.
- TOC, captions, cross-references as usual.

### Block options

- `#| standalone: true`, required: the block is a complete app.
- `#| components: [editor]`: show/hide the code editor and viewer.
- `#| viewerHeight: 420`: panel height in px.
- `#| layout: vertical`: stack editor above viewer.
- A live gallery of every option: <https://www.royfrancis.com/quarto-exp/documents/shinylive/>

### Including code files

App logic in a separate `.R` file? Paste it into the block with a **Quarto shortcode**, rather
than `source()`-ing it: copy-paste plays far better with Shinylive's in-browser file system.

````markdown
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
{{</* include app.R */>}}
```
````

:::

## Deployment: static hosts

A rendered report is **plain files**, so any **static web host** works. Quarto has native commands:

::: {.codewindow .bash width="80%"}
terminal
```bash
quarto publish gh-pages      # GitHub Pages
quarto publish quarto-pub    # free Posit cloud service
quarto publish netlify       # custom domains
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Before sharing, treat the service worker as a project resource, or collaborators may see a blank page:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    resources:
      - shinylive-sw.js
```
:::

## Try it now {.light background-color="#F1EEE6"}

::: {.hands-on}
**In `labs/lab-04-shinylive-quarto.qmd`:**

1. Create `report.qmd` with the extension enabled and one `{shinylive-r}` block (the histogram above).
2. `quarto render` → open the HTML. Confirm the widget runs **in the browser**.
3. Add a second interactive block and cross-reference a static figure.
4. (Stretch) Deploy the folder holding `report.html` to GitHub Pages or Netlify and share the URL.
:::

## A word on privacy and data

Because everything runs in the reader's browser, **uploaded data stays local**, true of a
standalone app and of a `{shinylive-r}` block in a report alike:

- Files are read into browser memory; they are **never transmitted** to the static host.
- Reader A's uploaded data is invisible to reader B; closing the tab discards it.
- This makes Shinylive an excellent fit for **sensitive or GDPR-relevant data**.

::: {.callout-caution}
The flip side: **your code is public** (it is downloaded to run). Never ship API keys,
passwords, or proprietary algorithms in a Shinylive app or report.
:::

## Two routes, one goal

Both routes end in **plain static files**; the reader's browser does the computing.

## Choosing an interactivity engine

There is no single right answer. Match the engine to the job:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-engine
#| tbl-cap: "Choosing an interactivity engine"
#| echo: false
gt_dark(data.frame(
  Engine    = c("**Quarto + Shinylive**", "**Observable JS (OJS)**", "**Traditional Shiny**"),
  Hosting   = c("Static", "Static", "Live server"),
  `Best for` = c("Small data, open work", "Dashboards, JS plots", "Big data, all packages"),
  Drawback  = c("Cold start, package limits", "You write JS", "Server cost and ops"),
  check.names = FALSE),
  font_size = 28
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
Roughly:

- **static (Shinylive/OJS)** = free, private by architecture, but browser-bound.
- **Server Shiny** = full power, more cost and ops. Most productions mix both.
:::

## Limitations to remember

Be honest about the trade-offs before committing to Shinylive:

::: {.incremental .highlight-last}
- **Load time**: first visit downloads webR + packages; expect a multi-second start.
- **Package availability**: only WASM-built packages work; no system libs, no raw sockets.
- **Network**: no direct databases; HTTP calls are subject to the host's cross-origin resource-sharing (CORS) rules.
- **Data size**: ship data to the browser, so keep payloads small (a few MB max).
- **Secrecy**: the code your reader can run is code they can read.
:::

## Automating deployment with GitHub Actions

Manual publishing is fine for a first pass. For reproducibility, automate it.

Two idiomatic options:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Standalone app → Pages

A reusable workflow (`posit-dev/r-shinylive`, `deploy-app.yaml`) runs on push:

- installs R + packages (renv), runs `shinylive::export(".", "site")`,
- uploads the `site/` artifact to GitHub Pages with proper `pages` / `id-token` write permissions.

### Quarto doc → Pages

- `quarto publish gh-pages` from a workflow;
- Or:

  - `quarto add quarto-ext/shinylive`
  - `quarto render` then a Pages deploy action.

:::

## The workflow in skeleton

::: {.codewindow width="100%"}
::: {.editor .yaml name="deploy-app.yaml"}
```yaml
name: Deploy app
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Export Shinylive site
        run: Rscript -e 'renv::restore(); shinylive::export(".", "site")'
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with: { path: "site" }
  deploy:
    needs: build
    permissions: { pages: write, id-token: write }
    environment: { name: github-pages, url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }} }
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5
```
:::

::: {.editor .yaml .fragment name="deploy-report.yaml"}
```yaml
name: Deploy report
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - name: Render report
        run: quarto render report.qmd
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with: { path: "_output" }
  deploy:
    needs: build
    permissions: { pages: write, id-token: write }
    environment: { name: github-pages }
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5
```
:::
:::
